Daily Debrief · Thursday, November 19, 2026
The S&P 500 was up 1.3% this morning and closed down 2%: Anthropic's debut pulled money out of the AI trade, and Nvidia made a new low.

Sixth straight loss for the index, and the ugliest one: a gap up, then a slide into the close with 464 of 500 stocks red. Everything on the list fell except Intel. The paper KO call stopped out; the NVDA put opened at the close.

The miss first. The paper KO $100 call stopped out intraday for −$128. We bought it Monday on the close, four cents over its trigger, after KO tagged a new high at $100.56. It never made another one: three sessions later KO traded $96.19, under the $97.38 stop, and closed $96.09. A breakout that can't hold its first day over the old high is a warning; we treated it as a trigger. Also: my locked SPY call for the week (above $754.37 on Friday, with $744–745 holding) is lost. SPY is $38 under it. Friday grades it.

What mattered today
  1. The reversal: the S&P 500 traded up to about 7,416 (+1.3%) and closed 7,175.83 (−2.0%), its sixth loss in a row and 8.2% under the October record. The Dow lost 1,101 points.
  2. Anthropic's debut: opened $111.50, closed $97.17 (+17% on the IPO price). The AI trade sold off around it: AMZN −3.9%, GOOGL −3.5%, CoreWeave from +10% to −6%.
  3. Nvidia: a new 52-week low at $145.71 after being up 4.7% early; Congress asked for briefings. AMD −7.7% on a short-seller report.
  4. Data: the Philly Fed survey fell to 6.3 (about 20 expected) while its prices-paid line jumped to 58.2. Continuing jobless claims rose 70,000. Goolsbee: inflation is "way higher" than 2%.
  5. Walmart beat and raised and fell 1%. After the close Intuit (−10% or more) and Ross (−5% or more) fell on soft guidance.
  6. The paper book: the KO call stopped out (−$128); the NVDA trigger held into the close, so the NVDA $140 put opened and the DAL $90 call was swapped out to make room (−$482).
Top 3 actionable
  1. NVDA Dec 18 $140 put (opened at the close, $612.50): still under $148.80 after a failed bounce at your 0.5; R:R 1.8 to 1; liquid (OI 28,999); lines up with the AI unwind.
  2. AMZN Dec 18 $245 put on a break under $255.00: lost your 2.382 and stalled under your 2.618 twice; R:R 2.2 to 1; liquid (OI 10,748); same AI unwind, Anthropic is the trigger.
  3. V Dec 18 $405 put: take target 1 at $392.38: it's $9.87 away with your 2.0 and the 50-day stacked there; liquid enough (OI 700, vol 544); lines up with the card-data hack and the broad selling.

Key numbers: oil (USO) flat on the day; 10-yr 5.05% (−2bp); 2-yr 4.77% (−3bp); dollar flat near its high; gold about $3,625 (−2.7%); VIX 27.98 (+14%).

Stocks fell 2%, yet the 2-year yield fell 3 basis points, the 10-year 2, and gold dropped 2.7%. When gold falls on a fear day, it usually means people are selling what they can, not hiding in it: that's forced selling, and the VIX jumping 14% to 27.98 says the same. Falling yields on weak data would normally help small caps and long-duration tech; today they didn't, which tells me this was about positioning in the AI trade, not about rates. Oil was flat, so it gave OXY and XOM nothing either way.

What's going on
Five events, each with the evidence
1. The reversal: the AI trade met its supply

My read: today was a positioning flush in AI, set off by the biggest new AI stock ever arriving on the market. I'm fairly sure of the shape (the selling hit the AI names hardest and started around the debut), less sure it's over. What would change my mind: the S&P back over Wednesday's close (7,323) within two sessions.

What we saw. The S&P 500 opened above Wednesday's close, reached about 7,416 (+1.3%) and closed 7,175.83 (−147.80, −2.0%), near the low. The Philadelphia chip index went from +4.7% to −2.4%; Nvidia from +4.7% to −3.3%; CoreWeave from +10.5% to −6.1% (TheStreet, AP). Breadth was one-sided: 38 S&P stocks rose, 464 fell, and 87% of NYSE volume traded down (TheStreet). All 11 sectors fell, consumer discretionary (−3.0%) and communication services (−2.9%) the most: that's where Amazon and Alphabet live.

Why. Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion and 853 million shares changed hands on day one. Yahoo reported retail selling other stocks to buy it; the losses deepened around its first trade just before noon. Its two biggest holders, Amazon (about 15%) and Alphabet (about 14%, per PitchBook), fell 3.9% and 3.5%. If you can now own the AI lab itself, you need the proxies less. That's the cleanest explanation I can find; no source names one single trigger.

What would prove it wrong: a quick rebound in AMZN and GOOGL while Anthropic keeps sliding (it fell to $95.69 after hours). Our names: NVDA, AMZN, GOOGL, PLTR, SMH, AMD.

2. The data: factories cooled, but prices didn't

Philly Fed headline 6.3 vs 20.0 expected (prior 20.9); new orders −0.4 (prior 4.3); prices paid 58.2 (prior 43.2).

My read: this is the uncomfortable mix, slower activity with sticky prices, and it keeps the Fed hiking into a slowdown. Fairly sure on the direction.

The numbers. Philly Fed manufacturing fell to 6.3 against about 20 expected (prior 20.9), a six-month low, with new orders at −0.4. Its prices-paid index jumped to 58.2 from 43.2, the highest since April. Initial jobless claims were 203,000 (about 197,000 expected); continuing claims rose 70,000 to 1.763 million, the biggest weekly rise since January 2024 (Reuters, investingLive).

The Fed. Chicago's Goolsbee said inflation is "way higher" than the 2% target and called AI spending a "pig through the python" that risks overheating (investingLive). Futures put a December hike near 94% (CME FedWatch via Investing.com). Waller speaks at 8:25 a.m. Friday; he said Wednesday "you have to go 50 in December."

What it means for the plays. A hiking Fed into slowing data is bad for expensive growth: that supports the paper PLTR, NVDA and INTC puts and the AMZN and GOOGL put ideas. It's a headwind for the AAPL and HLT calls, which need the index to steady. It doesn't change OXY. What would prove it wrong: a soft October PCE on Nov 25.

What management sees. CEO John Furner called the shopper "stable and resilient," with the share gains strongest among upper-income households. About 7,700 price rollbacks are running, partly paid for by tariff refunds.

What the market heard. CNBC called the raise "tepid"; Reuters called the sales outlook disappointing. A stock priced for perfection needs more than a small raise, and the after-hours tape agreed: Intuit beat ($2.91 vs $2.70) but guided under the Street and fell 10–14%; Ross beat but guided Q4 under and fell 5–9%; Gap cut its year and rose 4%.

My read: the consumer is fine; the price of owning consumer stocks is the problem. Our names: none directly; it argues against reading AMZN's drop as a retail problem. It's an AI-proxy problem.

4. Nvidia: a new low, and Washington is asking questions

What happened. NVDA was up 4.7% early, ran to $158.13, failed under your 0.5 ($155.33) and closed $145.98 (−3.3%), a new 52-week low ($145.71). The House Energy and Commerce Committee asked for a briefing by Dec 2; House Intelligence interviews are set with Huang on Dec 1. Reuters, citing the WSJ, says the SEC is looking at disclosures. Piper Sandler cut its target to $230, Jefferies to $250; Summit Insights downgraded to Hold; Bank of America stayed at Buy ($280).

AMD −7.7% to $489.19 after Hunterbrook disclosed a short, citing China export-control exposure. Intel +1.9%, the only real gainer on the list, on its first outside 18A foundry customer and Microsoft as a packaging customer.

My read: the governance and probe stories don't resolve in a day, and a stock with no permanent CEO doesn't get a premium back quickly. What would prove it wrong: NVDA back over $148.80 and then $155.33.

5. Visa and the banks: a data breach on a bad day

Visa (−3.1%), Mastercard and JPMorgan fell after disclosing that customer data was reached through a vendor hack (TheStreet, Yahoo). It's a small part of the index move but a big part of V's: V traded $400.74, $8.36 from the paper put's target 1. Our names: V.

AMD, SHOP and the AI proxies led the way down; INTC was the only name on the list up more than 1%.

Lesson of the day
SPY: the bearish outside day

An outside day is a candle whose high is above the prior day's high and whose low is below the prior day's low. When it closes near its low, it's a bearish outside day: buyers had the whole morning and lost all of it, plus the prior day's ground.

SPY today: Wednesday ranged $726.80–735.06. Thursday opened $737.46, went to $739.90 (above Wednesday's high), then fell to $715.65 (below Wednesday's low) and closed $715.87, 22 cents off the low. Volume was 1.5 times the 20-day average. Three things make this one count: it came after a confirmed double top, it closed through the 200-day, and the volume was heavy.

What it means for us: the day's high ($739.90) becomes the line. Bounces that stay under it are selling chances, and calls on index-sensitive names wait. It's also why NVDA and AMZN, which made the same candle, carry the put ideas tonight.

Practice: on your daily and 2-day charts of SPY, NVDA and AMZN, mark every outside day since September and note which ones closed at an extreme. We'll compare what happened next.

IWM: picking the swing decides the level

Levels: $304.38 (0%) · $278.84 (38.2%, with the 50/200-day) · $270.94 (50%) · $263.05 (61.8%, highlighted) · $251.82 (78.6%).

The concept. A retracement is only as good as its two anchors. Use the true start and end of the move you care about: the lowest low and the highest high of the run, on the timeframe you trade, and don't skip a higher high to make the math prettier. Wicks vs closes: I anchor on wicks (the real extremes) and judge the level on closes.

The anchors. IWM's run: the Mar 30 low $237.50 → the Aug 14 high $304.38 (Webull's adjusted daily bars). The Nov 4 high ($286.17) is a lower high inside the decline, not the end of the run, so it isn't the anchor for this ladder.

The math. Range = 304.38 − 237.50 = $66.88. 38.2% = 304.38 − 66.88 × 0.382 = $278.84 (sits on the 50-day $278.88 and the 200-day $278.67: lost on Nov 16). 50% = $270.94 (lost Nov 17). 61.8% = 304.38 − 66.88 × 0.618 = $263.05. 78.6% = $251.82.
